query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid free‐energy evaluation approach that integrates active-learning machine-learning potentials with enhanced sampling techniques (such as replica exchange or metadynamics) will deliver near ab initio accuracy in computing complete fusion free energies (including vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling) while substantially reducing computational cost.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys near their fusion (high-temperature) conditions in both solid and liquid phases.
generation.intervention: Deploy an active-learning framework to train ML potentials using a minimal set of high-fidelity ab initio calculations and then employ enhanced sampling methods to efficiently explore the free energy landscapes of both phases.
generation.conditions: Temperature ranges near the fusion transition (approximately 0.9–1.1 T_m) and compositions extending from elemental and binary systems to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
generation.structural_mediator: The ML potential acts as the mediator by capturing the essential features (electronic, vibrational, and anharmonic effects) of the free energy landscape, while enhanced sampling ensures accurate phase-space exploration.
generation.mechanism: By substituting costly full-scale ab initio molecular dynamics with a trained ML potential and sophisticated sampling, the method reduces the number of expensive calculations while still resolving the detailed free energy differences between solid and fluid phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Substantial reduction in computational cost (potentially by orders of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio MD) while maintaining free energy and derived observables (e.g., fusion temperature, latent heat) within acceptable ab initio error margins; the approach should be faster than TOR-TILD, particularly for complex, multicomponent systems.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics evaluations and TOR-TILD free-energy computations in elemental and binary systems.
generation.boundary: The method is expected to be effective within temperature ranges near the fusion transition and for composition spaces that include simple elemental and binary systems as well as more complex high-entropy alloys; uncertainties increase if applied far from these conditions.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the ML potential’s ability to capture extreme anharmonicity and electron–vibration coupling in highly complex systems without further calibration; additional validation may be required for systems with unforeseen electronic or vibrational complexities.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a comparative study where the free-energy profiles and fusion properties (such as phase free energies, fusion temperature, and latent heat) are computed for selected elemental, binary, and high-entropy alloy systems using (i) full ab initio molecular dynamics, (ii) TOR-TILD, and (iii) the new hybrid ML-enhanced sampling method. Ensure that the same temperature and composition boundaries are used for all simulations.
measurements: Phase free energy differences across solid and liquid states
Contributions from vibrational entropy and anharmonic effects
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hybrid ML-enhanced sampling method produces free energies or derived fusion properties that differ significantly (i.e., beyond acceptable ab initio uncertainty limits) from the full ab initio MD results, or if the computational speedup is not at least one order of magnitude greater than explicit MD, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Clean energy production is the cornerstone of our time. Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. decision.trend: Early studies relied on full ab initio molecular dynamics to compute free energies with all relevant entropy terms, ensuring accuracy but at a very high computational cost. Subsequently, methods such as TOR-TILD were developed to increase throughput in elemental and binary systems, yet they show severe scaling issues in multicomponent, high‐entropy alloys. In short, the progression has been from complete first-principles evaluations to approximate free energy integration schemes that work well in simple systems but are inadequate for the combinatorial complexity of multicomponent materials.
decision.unsolved: The key unresolved challenge is how to accurately and cost-effectively compute free energies for both solid and liquid phases—including the full vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling—especially in multicomponent high-entropy systems where current methods either are computationally prohibitive (explicit ab initio MD) or lose efficiency (TOR-TILD).
decision.lever: Develop a hybrid free-energy evaluation approach that integrates active-learning machine-learning potentials with enhanced sampling techniques (e.g., replica exchange or metadynamics). This lever would use a minimal number of high-fidelity ab initio calculations to train ML potentials that capture electronic, vibrational, and anharmonic effects, then employ enhanced sampling to efficiently span both solid and liquid free energy landscapes.
decision.why: This approach logically follows the trend: by addressing the computational cost of explicit MD and the scaling limitations of TOR-TILD, it promises orders-of-magnitude speedup while maintaining near ab initio accuracy. Prior successes in elemental and binary systems using ML-enhanced sampling indicate that, when carefully trained and validated, such models can extend to complex, multicomponent systems within defined temperature (near fusion) and composition boundaries. A decisive benchmark would be the direct comparison of phase free energies and derived observables (e.g., fusion temperature, latent heat) against fully converged ab initio MD results; any significant disparity beyond acceptable error margins would falsify the hypothesis.
